newsitem.title: ALGERIA: FEATURE - Islam still has place in Algerian poll.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Islam still has place in Algerian poll.

text.p: Well before campaigning started for Algeria's June 5 general election, President Liamine Zeroual carefully engineered a political system to try to keep it distant from Islamic politicking.

The use of Islam, the faith of Algeria's 29 million people, to attract voters is illegal. So too are displays of religious trappings, both of which proved so powerful in the last general election nearly six years ago.
Then, the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) swept to a massive lead and the nation plunged into bloodshed after the authorities scrapped the poll. The FIS has been outlawed.
Now, in the first general election since then, the battle between permitted Islamist-leaning parties and their adversaries shows the "Islamist card" still has a place in the poll.
One analyst, who followed most of the campaigning by the leading Islamist party, that of Mahfoud Nahnah, said the former Hamas party has skillfully kept the Islamist message alive.

And a former prime minister, anti-Islamist Redha Malek who heads the Republic National Alliance (ANR) says legal Islamist party supporters are still spreading what he termed Moslem fundamentalist propaganda at schools and universities.
The analyst, who asked not to be named, said of Nahnah's party: "The party supporters are well-disciplined, tightly keeping their militant feelings to themselves.

"Sympathisers and party workers were mobilised to go smoothly for a big share in the parliament, then more control in elected local government as stages to bring the party leader to the presidency in the next election."
In 1995, Nahnah won one-third of the votes, coming second to Zeroual in Algeria's multi-candidate presidential election.

Malek says legal Islamists are a threat to Algeria's social cohesion. "Our country's problem is not only with terrorism but with religious fundamentalism," he told a campaign rally on the outskirts of the Algerian capital.
ISLAMISTS PRUNE RELIGIOUS REFERENCES

Nahnah's party, newly named Movement for a Peaceful Society (MPS) replacing its Hamas-Movement of Islamic Society, appears to be toeing the new political line. Its platform reads like a modern social liberal party, pruned of Islamist references.
Nahnah himself insists he wants a rainbow parliament, representing all Algeria's political spectrum.
But in a first test over Algerian women's rights, the ideological fault lines swiflty put Islamists and their conservative allies on collision course with liberals and secularists.
"The women's law emanates from the Koran, and claims to change it is rebellion against Allah," said Abdallah Djaballah, leader of the second legal Islamist-oriented Nahda party.

One of Nahnah's women supporters, Hassiba Amokrane, running for a seat in parliament, said demands by advocates of westernised women's rights to change the law on women were trying to "break the Moslem nation's spine".

On the other side, the moderate secularist National Democratic Rally (RND), grouping Zeroual's supporters, promised women it will modify the sharia (Islamic law)-inspired law "to protect woman rights and human dignity through parliament".
Hawkish secular party candidates have pledged that if they are elected they will scrap the law altogether, saying it is a legal straitjacket keeping women as "minors".
CONTINUING FEAR OF FUNDAMENTALISTS
After more than five years of bloodshed some secularists say they fear a future Turkish-style showdown if legal Islamists score well in the election.

"If Nahnah's party dominates parliament we can have here the same situation as in Ankara," said Hocine, a physician, alluding to Turkey's Islamist-led government under fire from the powerful military to trim Moslem fundamentalist militancy.

About 60,000 people died in the past five years of strife in Algeria and some secularists accuse the authorities of using fear of fundamentalism as a means of trying to stay in power and limiting their opponents activities.
"The rulers, with the aim of smashing pro-democratic ranks, bring out the fundamentalist card," said Said Saadi, leader of the anti-Islamist Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD).

Left-wing Workers Party leader Louisa Hanoune told a rally in Algiers' Bab el Oued Moslem fundamentalist stronghold "they said (Nahnah's) party is a threat but everyone knows that this party is participating in the government with two ministers".
She added: "The country's leaders raise the fundamentalist danger as farmers raise scarecrows to protect their orchards from hungry birds."
